lessonTitle: Kelvin-Planck and Clausius Statements of the Second Law

blocks.text: A ship's captain proposes to drive the vessel by extracting heat from the ocean, cooling the water a little and using the heat to turn the propeller. The ocean holds enormous energy, and the first law is satisfied, but the second law forbids the idea. This unit states exactly what the second law prohibits and how to test claims against it.

blocks.markdown: The first law only requires energy to balance. It does not say which way a process may run: a hot cup of coffee never cools by pushing heat into a warm room and then spontaneously becomes hotter, even though that would conserve energy. The **second law** captures this directionality through two equivalent statements.

blocks.title: Kelvin-Planck statement
blocks.text: It is impossible for any device operating in a cycle to receive heat from a single reservoir and produce a net amount of work. Every heat engine must reject some heat to a colder reservoir, so $\eta_{th}<1$ always.

blocks.title: Clausius statement
blocks.text: It is impossible to construct a device operating in a cycle whose only effect is the transfer of heat from a cooler body to a warmer body. A refrigerator needs a work input.

blocks.markdown: The two statements are **equivalent**: violating one means violating the other. Suppose a device violated Clausius by moving $Q_L$ from a cold reservoir to a hot one with no work. Couple it to an ordinary engine that takes $Q_H$ from the hot reservoir, rejects $Q_L$ to the cold one and produces $W=Q_H-Q_L$. The cold reservoir is returned to its original condition, because it gives $Q_L$ and receives $Q_L$ back. The combined device now takes $Q_H-Q_L$ from the hot reservoir alone and produces $W$, which violates Kelvin-Planck. A similar argument works in the reverse direction.

rows: $Q_H=W+Q_L$ for an engine; $Q_H=Q_L+W_{in}$ for a refrigerator
Does an engine reject heat to a colder reservoir?
Does a refrigerator have work input?
blocks.caption: A checklist for a claimed engine or refrigerator

blocks.title: Testing a claimed engine
blocks.prompt: An inventor claims an engine takes 500 kJ from a source at 800 K, produces 420 kJ of work and rejects 80 kJ to surroundings at 300 K. Is it possible?

steps.text: First law: does the energy balance close?
Maximum possible, the Carnot efficiency between 800 K and 300 K.

blocks.answer: The claimed efficiency of 84 % exceeds the Carnot limit of 62.5 %, so the engine is impossible even though it conserves energy.

blocks.title: Testing a claimed refrigerator
blocks.prompt: A refrigerator is claimed to remove 3.0 kW from a space at 270 K and reject 3.8 kW to a room at 300 K with 0.8 kW of work input. Is it possible?

steps.text: First law: 3.0 + 0.8 = 3.8, so the energy balance closes.
Carnot maximum between 270 K and 300 K.

blocks.answer: The claimed COP of 3.75 is below the limit of 9.0, so the device does not violate the second law; a real machine can approach but not reach the limit.

blocks.markdown: A process is **reversible** if it can be reversed so that both the system and its surroundings return exactly to their initial states. All real processes are **irreversible**. The factors that make a process irreversible are called irreversibilities. A cycle is reversible only if every process in it is reversible, and reversible engines are the most efficient ones, which is why they provide the benchmark.

rows: Work becomes internal energy that cannot spontaneously turn back into work
Heat transfer across a finite temperature difference
Heat flows only from hot to cold
Boiler tubes heated by a flame far hotter than the steam
Gas expands with no work done and cannot recompress itself
Gas rushing into a vacuum, throttling valve
Mixed fluids do not unmix spontaneously
Current through a resistance turns into heat
blocks.caption: Common sources of irreversibility

blocks.title: Idealisations
blocks.text: Reversible processes are limits: they require frictionless motion, infinitesimal temperature differences and infinitely slow change. No real device is reversible, but the idea tells us the best that could be achieved.

blocks.title: Energy conservation is not enough
blocks.text: A claim that conserves energy can still violate the second law. Always apply the first-law check first, then the second-law checks.

points: Kelvin-Planck: no cyclic device can convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work.
Clausius: no cyclic device can move heat from cold to hot with no other effect.
The statements are equivalent; violating one lets you build a device that violates the other.
To test a claim, check the first-law balance, the presence of rejected heat or work input, and the Carnot limit.
Friction, finite-temperature-difference heat transfer, unrestrained expansion and mixing are common irreversibilities.

questions.stem: Which statement is the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law?

options.text: Heat cannot flow spontaneously from a cold body to a hot body
No cyclic device can receive heat from a single reservoir and produce net work
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
Every engine has an efficiency of 100 % in the ideal limit

questions.correctOptionText: No cyclic device can receive heat from a single reservoir and produce net work

distractorRationale.a: That is closer to the Clausius statement.
distractorRationale.d: This is false, even for reversible engines.

questions.explanation: Kelvin-Planck says a heat engine must reject heat to a second, colder reservoir; it cannot convert all its heat input to work. Clausius is the refrigerator counterpart.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a source of irreversibility?

options.text: Heat transfer across an infinitesimally small temperature difference
A frictionless quasi-equilibrium expansion
Heat transfer across a large temperature difference
A frictionless compression with no heat transfer

questions.correctOptionText: Heat transfer across a large temperature difference
questions.explanation: Heat transfer across a finite temperature difference cannot be reversed without a refrigerator. The other options describe idealised reversible processes.

questions.stem: An inventor's engine receives 100 kJ of heat from a single furnace and produces 100 kJ of work in a cycle, rejecting no heat. What is wrong?

options.text: It violates the first law
It violates the Kelvin-Planck statement
It violates the Clausius statement directly
Nothing: it is a perfect engine

questions.explanation: The first law is satisfied because energy in equals work out. But a cycle that converts all heat from one reservoir into work is what Kelvin-Planck prohibits, so the device is impossible.

questions.stem: What can be said if a device is found to violate the Clausius statement?

options.text: It can be combined with an ordinary heat engine to violate the Kelvin-Planck statement
It has no consequence for Kelvin-Planck
It conserves energy and so is possible
It must be a reversible device

questions.correctOptionText: It can be combined with an ordinary heat engine to violate the Kelvin-Planck statement
questions.explanation: Pairing a Clausius violator with an engine that rejects the same heat Q_L to the cold reservoir leaves the cold reservoir unchanged and yields net work from the hot reservoir alone. That is a Kelvin-Planck violation, showing the two statements are equivalent.

questions.stem: A claimed engine takes 900 kJ from a source at 600 K, produces 400 kJ of work and rejects 500 kJ to surroundings at 300 K. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: Impossible, because it violates the first law
Impossible, because its efficiency of 44 % exceeds the Carnot limit of 50 %
Possible: efficiency 44 % is below the Carnot limit of 50 %, so the engine is irreversible but allowed
Possible only if it is reversible

questions.correctOptionText: Possible: efficiency 44 % is below the Carnot limit of 50 %, so the engine is irreversible but allowed

distractorRationale.d: A reversible engine would have exactly 50 %, so this one is irreversible.

questions.explanation: The first-law check balances, and the claimed efficiency 400/900 = 0.444 is below the reversible limit 1 - 300/600 = 0.50. A real, irreversible engine has an efficiency below the limit, so this claim is plausible.

questions.stem: A heat engine in a cycle takes 750 kJ of heat from a source and produces 300 kJ of net work. Find the heat rejected to the sink in kJ.
questions.explanation: For a cycle the net work equals the net heat, so Q_L = Q_H - W = 750 - 300 = 450 kJ. The first law fixes the rejected heat, and Kelvin-Planck requires it to be positive.

questions.stem: A claimed refrigerator keeps a space at 255 K in a 300 K room and consumes 2 kW of power. What is the maximum heat removal rate it could achieve in kW?
questions.explanation: The Carnot COP is 255/(300 - 255) = 5.667. The maximum heat removal rate is COP x W = 5.667 x 2 = 11.33 kW, and a claim above that value is impossible.

questions.stem: A reversible limit is used to test an engine that takes 1800 kJ from a source at 600 K and rejects heat to a sink at 300 K. What is the smallest heat that could possibly be rejected, in kJ?
questions.explanation: The best case is a reversible engine with Q_L/Q_H = T_L/T_H, so Q_L,min = 1800 x 300/600 = 900 kJ. Any claimed rejection below this value would imply an efficiency above Carnot and is impossible.

questions.stem: State the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements. Show that a hypothetical device which violates the Clausius statement could be combined with a normal heat engine to violate the Kelvin-Planck statement.
markingGuide: Kelvin-Planck: no cyclic device receives heat from a single reservoir and produces net work
Clausius: no cyclic device has the sole effect of transferring heat from a cold to a hot body
Clausius violator moves Q_L from cold to hot with no work
Engine takes Q_H from hot, rejects Q_L to cold, produces W = Q_H - Q_L
Cold reservoir is unchanged overall, so the combination takes net heat Q_H - Q_L from the hot reservoir alone and produces work, violating Kelvin-Planck
questions.explanation: The coupled system exchanges heat with the hot reservoir only, because the cold reservoir gains and loses the same Q_L. Its only effect is to convert heat into work, which is exactly what Kelvin-Planck forbids.

questions.stem: Define a reversible process and list four sources of irreversibility in real thermal systems. Explain why the reversible cycle is used as the benchmark for real engines.
markingGuide: Reversible: can be reversed so that both system and surroundings return exactly to the initial state
Any four sources: friction, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, unrestrained expansion, mixing, electric resistance, chemical reaction
Real processes always contain some of these irreversibilities
Reversible engines are the most efficient possible between two reservoirs
So their efficiency is the upper limit against which real engines are compared
questions.explanation: A reversible process is an idealised limit with no friction, no finite temperature differences and no unrestrained expansion. Because such cycles give the highest efficiency possible, they set the benchmark for real engines.
